title: Micah 5:7–15
context: The prophet describes “the remnant of Jacob” among the nations, both “like dew from the LORD” that brings life and like a lion that no one can withstand, and prays that Israel’s enemies be cut off. Then the LORD speaks, promising that “in that day” he will cut off horses, chariots, strongholds, witchcraft, images, pillars, and Asherah poles, so that the people no longer trust in military power or “the work of your hands,” and will bring vengeance on the nations that did not listen. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground: God purifies his people of false trust and idolatry, and the remnant lives by his gift rather than its own strength.

verses.text: The remnant of Jacob will be among many peoples like dew from the LORD, like showers on the grass, that don’t wait for man nor wait for the sons of men.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The remnant of Jacob will be among many peoples like dew from the LORD, like showers on the grass.” Arminian readers note that the remnant brings blessing among the nations.

Dew comes from God, not from human effort.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the remnant’s life as God’s gift, which “don’t wait for man.”

Shared ground: both traditions read the image as hope: the people God preserves become a source of refreshment among many peoples.

verses.text: The remnant of Jacob will be among the nations, among many peoples, like a lion among the animals of the forest, like a young lion among the flocks of sheep; who, if he goes through, treads down and tears in pieces, and there is no one to deliver.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The remnant of Jacob will be among the nations, among many peoples, like a lion among the animals of the forest.” Arminian readers note the contrast with the dew image.

The remnant will also be strong and unafraid.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read the lion image as God’s protection and vindication of his people.

Shared ground: both traditions read the strong imagery soberly as poetry about security under God, not as a license for violence.

verses.text: Let your hand be lifted up above your adversaries, and let all of your enemies be cut off.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Let your hand be lifted up above your adversaries, and let all of your enemies be cut off.” Arminian readers note the prayer or wish for victory over enemies.

The speaker may be addressing Israel or the LORD; readers take it both ways.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hold the addressee lightly.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as hope for deliverance from oppressors, which the LORD’s words in 5:10–15 then take up.

verses.text: “It will happen in that day”, says the LORD, “that I will cut off your horses from among you and will destroy your chariots.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “I will cut off your horses from among you and will destroy your chariots.” Arminian readers note that God removes the military power his people trusted.

The cutting off is aimed at false security.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God stripping away what competes with trust in him (cf. Ps 20:7).

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the LORD’s people are to rely on him rather than on armies or alliances.

verses.text: I will cut off the cities of your land and will tear down all your strongholds.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I will cut off the cities of your land and will tear down all your strongholds.” Arminian readers note that fortified cities are also removed.

The theme of false trust continues.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God removing human defenses so that his people depend on him.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as purification rather than mere destruction, preparing a people who trust the LORD.

verses.text: I will destroy witchcraft from your hand. You shall have no soothsayers.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I will destroy witchcraft from your hand. You shall have no soothsayers.” Arminian readers note that occult practices are named alongside military trust.

Both are ways of seeking security apart from God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the removal of forbidden practices (cf. Deut 18:10–12).

Shared ground: both traditions agree that God’s people are to seek guidance from him, not from sorcery or omens.

verses.text: I will cut off your engraved images and your pillars from among you; and you shall no more worship the work of your hands.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I will cut off your engraved images and your pillars from among you; and you shall no more worship the work of your hands.” Arminian readers note the end of idolatry.

The phrase “the work of your hands” exposes idols as human-made.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the first commandment restored in practice.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that worshiping what human hands make is folly, and that the LORD’s purification frees his people from it.

verses.text: I will uproot your Asherah poles from among you; and I will destroy your cities.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I will uproot your Asherah poles from among you; and I will destroy your cities.” Arminian readers note that the sacred poles of Canaanite worship are removed.

The cleansing reaches every place of false worship.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God’s thorough removal of idolatry.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the LORD’s work of making his people holy, not as an end in itself.

verses.text: I will execute vengeance in anger and wrath on the nations that didn’t listen.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “I will execute vengeance in anger and wrath on the nations that didn’t listen.” Arminian readers note that the nations’ judgment is tied to their refusal to listen.

God’s justice reaches beyond Israel.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God as judge of all nations.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the LORD’s judgment is just, and both note that Micah 4:1–5 also pictures nations coming to learn his ways, named without harmonizing.
